webTitle: Bond market rebuffs US treasury’s plan to buy back $6bn in government debt

fields.headline: Bond market rebuffs US treasury’s plan to buy back $6bn in government debt
fields.trailText: Scott Bessent made announcement on Wednesday as bond yields rose to highest point since 2008 financial crisis
fields.bodyText: The US treasury moved to cut the cost of borrowing on Wednesday only to be swiftly rebuffed by the bond market. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, announced the US would buy back $6bn worth of government debt – treasuries – in an effort to alleviate a selloff in the US bond market that has put pressure on interest rates. But the size of the deal failed to appease bond buyers and the yield on 10-year treasuries rose to a three-year high. Rising inflation and uncertainty from the war in Iran have spooked investors from US bonds, historically known to be one of the safest investment vehicles. Treasury yields have been rising, with the yield for the 30-year treasury bond hitting about 5.2% – the highest yield since the 2008 financial crisis. In an attempt to alleviate the bond market, Bessent on 19 August announced the treasury would at least double its typical buyback operation. The move is meant to stabilize the market: fewer bonds on the market should mean that yields go down. But in the weeks since the announcement, treasury yields have continued to rise. Even after Bessent announced the operation would target $6bn worth of government bonds, yields on Wednesday continued to rise. In August, US government debt for the first time in the country’s history reached $40tn – double the amount of debt from just 10 years ago. Higher yields could ultimately mean higher interest rates on loans, including mortgages, student debt and car loans, as these loans are often tied to the bond market. The move puts more pressure on the US Federal Reserve to deal with inflation, which has been pushed up by the war in Iran. The annualized inflation rate hit a three-year high in May before going down to 3.4% in July – 0.7% higher than the same time last year – largely because of higher energy prices. Donald Trump on Wednesday warned that oil prices were unlikely to come down before the midterm election. Though Iran “can’t hold out any longer”, its leaders are “desperate to try and affect the election”, he said. “Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump predicted. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose past $100 for the first time since July on Wednesday as conflict in the Middle East continued to escalate. The Fed could raise interest rates to mitigate higher prices, at the risk of upsetting the White House. Last week, Trump said the Fed “must get smart” and lower interest rates. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE,” he wrote on social media. The pressure puts the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, who stepped into the role in May, in a bind: manage inflation or face the president’s wrath. In a closely watched speech at the Fed’s Jackson Hole symposium in August, Warsh affirmed that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”, but held off on whether the the central bank would raise rates anytime soon.

webTitle: The Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanity | Editorial

fields.headline: The Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanity
fields.trailText: Editorial: The US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel bills
fields.bodyText: Imperialism does not require a flag to be planted or a governor dispatched. It can be a powerful nation deciding who governs a smaller, weaker country, and on what terms and for whose benefit its resources will be developed. Donald Trump’s kidnapping of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro, putting his deputy – Delcy Rodríguez – in his place as president, and then her signing a deal handing a fifth of the country’s proven oil reserves to the US, amount to a modern version of 19th-century gunboat diplomacy. Regime change supplied America’s commercial concession. This won’t bother Mr Trump. But it should. The US president has oversold his neocolonial spoils. The additional production Venezuela is supposed to bring online might bring down oil prices eventually, but not anytime soon. Crucially, what Mr Trump calls “the biggest oil deal in history” won’t cause the price at the pump to fall before November’s midterms. When so many American voters are struggling to pay energy bills, it’s hard to see how unrealised Orinoco Belt riches are going to help Republican candidates. The US president also promotes the idea that he is transforming the US’s industrial landscape through fossil fuels. Although the Venezuela oil grab might be highly profitable for a few selected companies, the windfall is dwarfed by the size of the US economy. Mr Trump is not getting cheap energy but a spectacle of American power. That may be enough for him. Before Mr Maduro was captured, Mr Trump had decided that Venezuela’s oil belonged to the US. The Venezuelan strongman was offered exile if he gave Washington want it wanted. When he dithered, a US armada assembled off Venezuela’s coast. Yet Mr Trump did not replace Mr Maduro with María Corina Machado from the democratic opposition. He instead backed the authoritarian regime that could secure the oilfields from ambitious army generals and spare the costs of occupation. The US doesn’t rule Venezuela directly, but it is exercising power through a lifelong socialist, Ms Rodríguez. She is remaking Chavismo, the revolutionary movement launched by Hugo Chávez, in her image – enraging some leftists. Ms Rodríguez has granted North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep) concessions to 17 oilfields in Venezuela for decades to come. Nabep’s boss, Alejandro Betancourt, a controversial Venezuelan oil billionaire, popped up in Caracas for this week’s visit by the US energy secretary, Chris Wright. Nabep has in turn granted the Pentagon a 35% equity stake at no cost to the US taxpayer. The charge of “Yankee imperialism” was often dismissed as kneejerk anti-Americanism. Mr Trump has turned it into an American boast. Ms Rodríguez argues that she is no puppet. Cooperation with Mr Trump, she says, will bring Venezuela investment and could generate $200bn in oil revenues. Unequal bargains have often benefited local rulers and intermediaries. The question is: what kind of economy and social order will that revenue produce? Oil cash is not the same as sovereign development. Mr Trump is a playground bully handed the world’s most powerful military. He mistakes coercion for greatness and sovereign nations for toys. He uses US power to feed his bottomless ego – recently claiming himself to be a bigger historical figure than Caesar, Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Stalin and Mao. When he departs the stage, others will have to rebuild what he has squandered: the US’s authority, its alliances and its reputation. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in our letters section, please click here.

webTitle: Republicans kick off ‘midterm convention’ to overcome Trump unpopularity

fields.headline: Republicans kick off ‘midterm convention’ to overcome Trump unpopularity
fields.trailText: GOP plans to center the president at rare two-day Texas event as party hopes to retain control of House in midterms
fields.bodyText: Republicans are gathering in Texas on Wednesday for a rare “midterm convention”, as they attempt to convince Americans to vote for a party led by a deeply unpopular president who has overseen inflation and led the US into an increasingly unpopular war. Donald Trump will dominate the two-day convention, appearing both nights as the GOP works to cling to control of the House of Representatives in November. Republicans plan to put the president at the center of the event, a bold strategy given his approval rating is hovering at about 38%, while accusing the Democratic party of being socialist and out of touch with Americans. However, in a sign of Trump’s toxicity, some vulnerable Republicans have said they will not attend the Dallas event: risking the potential ire of the president, but avoiding a public association with a deeply unpopular leader. Less than two months out from the midterm elections, the Republican party faces a serious battle to retain its slender control of the House, while Democrats are increasingly hopeful they could pick up Senate seats. Winning either would put the Democratic party in position to stymie Trump’s aims during his final two years in office. The convention represents perhaps Republicans’ final opportunity to make a large-scale, high-profile pitch to Americans. Joe Gruters, the chair of the Republican National Committee (RNC), which is organizing the convention, said the program would attempt to demonstrate how Republicans are “lowering costs, securing our border, making our communities safer, and putting American workers and families first”. Whether voters buy that is a different matter, given costs, including gas prices, have risen during Trump’s presidency. Forecasters give Republicans a slim chance of holding on to the House, in particular, and some members of Congress have been keen to distance themselves from the event. Several Republican members of Congress said they will skip it entirely. Some Democrats are congregating in Dallas to counter the convention’s narrative. On Wednesday, JB Pritzker, the Illinois governor, joined a Texas Democratic party event and accused Republicans stumping for Trump of “bootlicking”. He also alleged that Trump’s efforts to enact restriction on mail-in voting amount to a promise to end fair elections in the future. “If Democrats don’t win, if they don’t win in this election, we may not have other elections,” Pritzker said. “Or certainly we’re going to have future elections, every single one of which will be rigged.” Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, said a contingent of Democrats on Thursday will “counter the falsehoods and extremism” on display in American Airlines Center. Republicans facing close re-election bids have proved particularly likely to dodge the event, mindful that their Democratic opponents are looking for any opportunity to tie them to Trump. Tom Barrett, facing a close re-election fight in Michigan, and Zach Nunn, locked in a tight race in Iowa, are among those who have said they won’t be in Texas, and on Thursday Axios reported that “only about 100 lawmakers and candidates are expected to attend”. As well as risking association with Trump, there was the issue of cost. Multiple reports have suggested that House Republicans were being asked to donate at least $25,000 to the party to get a ticket. Among the few who are confirmed to be attending are JD Vance and the former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, along with Ken Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate in Texas who is polling neck-and-neck with Democrat James Talarico in a state that hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. There are signs too, that enthusiasm is low among the rank and file. The RNC announced in mid-August that Americans could apply for tickets to attend the event, suggesting that applicants would enter a lottery, and only a lucky few would be granted access. Yet on Friday, days before the event was due to begin, applications for tickets were instantly being granted on an RNC sign-up page, suggesting the event was not yet at capacity. Should the attendance be lacklustre, it will be a clear indictment of Trump himself, given RNC marketing materials in the buildup had made it clear it was the president’s show. Indeed, some messages billed the event as “Trump’s midterm convention” – ditching the term ‘Republican’ altogether – while every press release has been at pains to stress Trump will be there both nights. Trump himself was bullish about the convention in a podcast interview last week, telling the Texas lieutenant governor, Dan Patrick: “It’s going to be big stuff.” Chris Hippensteel contributed reporting

webTitle: Iran claims to have attacked 10 ships near strait of Hormuz after US strikes

fields.headline: Iran claims to have attacked 10 ships near strait of Hormuz after US strikes
fields.trailText: Oil price rises above $100 a barrel as Tehran responds to US attacks that sunk five Iranian tankers
fields.bodyText: Tehran has said it attacked 10 ships around the strait of Hormuz after the US sunk five Iranian tankers, as escalating strikes between the two countries sent the oil price above $100 a barrel for the first time since July. The attacks were the sharpest flare-up of strikes in weeks, as the two sides struggled to break a deadlock in the six-month-long war. Fighting in recent weeks has largely revolved around who controls the strait of Hormuz, as Iran attempts to close off the waterway and Washington enforces a blockade of Iranian ports. The strait is a critical route for global energy supplies, with up to 20% of the world’s oil and gas transiting it before the US-Iran war. The rising price of oil, above the psychologically significant $100 mark, is likely to raise inflation and the price of goods. Stocks fell on Wall Street while rising fuel and food prices in the US will further frustrate the Trump administration, which faces a midterm election with an unpopular war and a cost-of-living crisis. Among the vessels struck by Iran were two US vessels and eight oil tankers, the Iranian’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Wednesday. The IRGC said the 10 vessels were “noncompliant” – a likely reference to ships that tried to traverse the waterway without its permission. At least one sailor was killed and another was missing. The US denied that its vessels were hit, with US Central Command saying on social media that all “attempted attacks failed”. A tanker in Iraqi waters carrying 2mi barrels of fuel oil was also struck by a drone, according to Iraqi officials. There were no reports of casualties among the crew and the Iraqi government said there were no reported oil leaks. Iran said it also fired missiles at US bases in Jordan – 18 of which authorities said were intercepted while two fell in unpopulated areas. The US had said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, publishing videos of ships on fire. The US military said the attacks were a response to Iran targeting a US navy warship twice in the previous two days. Iranian state TV said the US strikes had followed a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn” to seize a US underwater drone in the strait. The US said the seized craft was a “defective” older model that did not carry any sensitive data. The back-and-forth strikes signalled an intensifying escalation between the two sides as Washington announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers if Iran targets its warships. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, told reporters. Iran said it would also escalate its attacks, and that for every two or three tankers struck it would respond by hitting 20. The IRGC said it would also release maps of a new, much-larger area near the strait that it considers forbidden for ships to traverse, extending as far as the Gulf off Chabahar for the first time. The conflict has also taken on an increasingly regional dimension as the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen traded strikes with Saudi Arabia. The Houthis launched a wave of attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, causing large fires at oil installations and wounding 73 people. The Houthis said dozens of people have been killed in Saudi airstrikes, something unconfirmed by Riyadh. Fighting re-ignited between the two sides after the Houthis launched an offensive against the Saudi-backed government of Yemen in south Yemen last week, aimed at reaching the Red Sea. The group is trying to enforce a Red Sea blockade against Saudi Arabia, announced in July. If enforced, it would cut off another route for the kingdom to export its oil.

webTitle: Israel sanctions will not hurt intelligence sharing between spy agencies, says Miliband

fields.headline: Israel sanctions will not hurt intelligence sharing between spy agencies, says Miliband
fields.trailText: UK foreign secretary says international community including US shares ‘frustration’ at Israel’s failure to constrain illegal settlers
fields.bodyText: British intelligence has been given assurances by its Israeli counterpart that information sharing with the UK will continue as before, Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has said. The disclosure counters predictions that his decision to impose a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements would lead to a collapse in cooperation between the agencies. The exchanges of information are seen as mutually beneficial and it is understood that Israeli intelligence was never willing to become mired in any political dispute between the two governments. Miliband insists the intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank. Miliband also expressed confidence that the US shared some of his exasperation with Israel’s reluctance to constrain the settlers in the West Bank, or to engage fully with the 20-point plan for Gaza set out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. As yet there has been no explicit criticism of the UK’s actions by the White House. Trump avoided taking a hard stance when pressed about the coalition of countries, including the UK, France, and Canada, that have imposed new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank. “I’ll be speaking to Israel, I’ll be speaking to them, and I’ll find out what’s their thinking,” he said on Wednesday. Trump, now locked in fighting midterm elections, appears reluctant to leap to the aid of Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who persuaded him to go to war against Iran. That decision has pushed oil prices beyond $100 a barrel, helping to swell a threatened “blue wave” that could leave the Democrats in charge of both the House and the Senate. There is also cross-party concern in the US at the violent tactics adopted by some Israeli settlers. Miliband said on Sky News on Wednesday: “We obviously talked to the Americans in advance of our announcement. I think the whole international community, let me say this, has been quite frustrated, to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government. “I think there is real concern about what is happening … underlying so much of the conflicts in the Middle East is this failure to really grasp the situation between Israel and Palestine. “It’s in our interest to act not just because it’s standing up for our values, but because it’s in our interests to have this two-state solution as a rock of stability in the Middle East.” The US decision not to oppose the UK over its sanctions and ban on trade with the Israeli settlements follows conversations between Trump and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Monday, as well as previous diplomatic exchanges at lower levels. Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, was careful not to endorse the UK sanctions, but affirmed he shared the objective of securing greater stability. Miliband can also claim credit for persuading Canada and France to join the trade ban, the surprise element in the package announced on Tuesday. The agreement came together late in the process. Eight other European countries have announced their intention to introduce such measures or to support the measures within the EU, a statement of solidarity that represents probably less of a shift than headlines might suggest. Some of the signatory countries had already taken steps independent of the EU, or had long been advocating for measures such as suspension of the Israel-EU trade agreement. For France, the decision to join the British initiative was formalised relatively late during Emmanuel Macron’s trip to London, when he met Burnham on 3 September and celebrated the display of the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum. France acted after a Franco-Swedish proposal made to the EU27 in April appeared to be making little progress. The French plan aimed to establish an embargo or tariff on products from the occupied territories, but resistance from a constellation of countries including Germany, Italy and Bulgaria blocked progress. The commission also appeared to raise objections. Paris last year had led the push to recognise the state of Palestine as critical to the two-state solution, but much of the French diplomatic energy had subsequently drifted. The UK, along with Jordan, will hold a meeting concerning improving humanitarian supplies into Gaza at the UN general assembly later this month. In advance of Miliband’s statement, Trump had been hinting that he might support the Argentinian claim to sovereignty over the Falklands, a proposal mooted by Netanyahu’s son. But in a little-noticed move likely to please Washington, Miliband this week supplemented the action against Israel by announcing fresh nuclear-related sanctions against Iran, including targeting Iranian ships involved in “malign behaviour”. The UK also said it was backing a motion to be put to the UN stating Iran was in breach of its obligations on nuclear proliferation. The new sanctions are extended to cover energy, software, metals, gold and related activities such as shipping, insurance and banking. Most Iranian aircraft will be prohibited from landing in the UK. In response to the UK ban on goods, not due to come into force for at least six months, Israel has said it will: close the British consulate in in occupied East Jerusalem; remove British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel; terminate the UK’s role in training Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank; and deny 12 mainly leftwing MPs entry to Israel.

webTitle: Texas Republican in race for key House seat under fire for derogatory comments

fields.headline: Texas Republican in race for key House seat under fire for derogatory comments
fields.trailText: Brandon Herrera of state’s 23rd congressional district calls insults against women and unhoused people ‘jokes’
fields.bodyText: A Republican candidate for a key congressional district in Texas has come under scrutiny over a series of derogatory comments made about women in his social media posts and videos. Brandon Herrera, who is the GOP candidate for Texas’s 23rd congressional district, has made a string of insults while fashioning a rightwing online persona as the “AK Guy”, and hosts a YouTube channel with more than 4 million subscribers that tests and reviews firearms. The comments, first reported by CNN, include Herrera taking aim at people he opposes politically, and women. In a 2023 video, he said that a gun range dummy’s empty head was “full of mush – much like the average Austin feminist”, and in a separate 2024 video, he likened the weight of “angry blue-haired” feminists to that of orca whales and elephants. In 2020, Herrera filmed himself firing a gun at bottles of ranch dressing and, after they exploded, rubbing the condiment on to himself and declaring that this would “make me irresistible to the fat bitches”. While discussing the merits of a car on X in 2023, Herrera opined that “4 doors means more whores”. Other groups have also been the focus of Herrera’s online content. In 2020, while firing a gun at a ham, Herrera said that while purchasing a ham for target practice was expensive, it was “still cheaper than a homeless person”. This isn’t the first time that Herrera has come under scrutiny. In 2024, during a run for Congress, Herrera said: “I am not, nor have I never [sic] been, a neo-Nazi” after describing a Nazi-era gun as “the original ghetto blaster”. The Republican Jewish Coalition condemned him at the time as “a goose-stepping extremist”. Herrera said that all these comments were jokes, and took aim at his opponent in this November’s midterm election, Democrat Katy Padilla Stout. “It’s disappointing that CNN would allow someone to allege that jokes about feminism lead to violence when Stout is fighting to return children to the parent convicted of abusing them,” Herrera said in a statement to CNN, referring to a case in which Stout was appointed as a defense attorney for a father seeking to restore parental rights after a domestic abuse allegation. Asked to comment on his previous statements made online, Herrera said via his campaign that it was “disappointing” that “alleged journalists” would “ignore” the Stout case. He did not reference his own past statements. The past comments could add to Republicans’ challenge of holding on to the US House of Representatives seat. Herrera is attempting to replace Tony Gonzales, a Republican lawmaker who resigned in April amid a House ethics committee investigation into his relationship with a former aide. While Democrats havenot prevailed in this district since 2015, the party has recently added it to its target list and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has sent funding to Stout, a former teacher and attorney, in what is expected to be a strong year for Democrats amid rising voter dissatisfaction with Donald Trump.

webTitle: Texas was once a hotbed of wild west socialism – could it make a comeback?

fields.headline: Texas was once a hotbed of wild west socialism – could it make a comeback?
fields.trailText: Long before it became a rightwing political bastion the state was defined by cowboys on strike and farmers organizing
fields.bodyText: Texas is well-known as a Republican-red state, but it has another, largely forgotten red history of the radical shade. Long before it became a rightwing political stronghold, it was defined by cowboys on strike, farmers organizing against the railroads, and one of the largest Socialist party chapters in the country. “In Texas, the history of our radical politics and labor and working class tradition has been purposefully hidden,” author David Griscom said. “It’s important to go back and correct the record and see that there was an effort to try to make Texans forget the radical roots in the kind of more recent past.” That’s the project of Griscom’s first book, The Myth of Red Texas. The cowboys idolized by conservatives, for instance, fought for public land access during the fence-cutting wars of the 1880s. At that time, wealthy northerners and Europeans were entering the state. Their arrival coincided with the invention of barbed wire, which cowboys called “the devil’s rope”, explains Griscom, who co-hosts two leftist podcasts, Left Reckoning and The Jacobin Show, and is based in Austin. “People almost immediately saw barbed wire for what it was, which was a tool of dispossession,” said Griscom. “It almost immediately got used across the state by the wealthy big landowners who wanted to enclose more and more land and access to water in streams, but that ran up against an older tradition of the west as an open range.” As fences blocked access to grazing land, water and roads, groups of cowboys began cutting them down, organizing themselves into clandestine vigilante organizations with names like the Blue Devils and the Knights of the Knippers. Ordinary Texans largely supported the cowboy fence-cutters, but the backlash was swift. Rich ranchers complained to government officials, who sent the Texas rangers – a state-sanctioned police force – to crack down on them. In 1884, the governor called a special session of the state legislature, which declared fence-cutting to be felony punishable by up to five years in prison, while making it a misdemeanor to fence land that did not belong to you. “It really shows the unequal way that the state and the legal system were developing in Texas and what that was a response to,” said Griscom. “But notably, while these large landowners were trying to enclose more and more land as private property, they were still using the public grasslands to raise their cattle. They were very happy to use the public lands while trying to restrict people’s access.” During the same period, cowboys also fought for labor rights as ranchers began hiring them to work on their newly privatized land – and paying them low wages. A group of those cowboys banded together and went on strike in 1883. Many Texas history books, Griscom said, assert that the new labor activists spent all their time getting drunk at the saloon, spending their entire strike fund. But according to the US commissioner of labor’s official report on the strike, the author said, the cowboys actually won their demands. Despite crackdowns from the government and wealthy capitalists, Texans kept organizing for their rights, including by forming the third-largest socialist party in the nation by the early 1900s. “Whenever you see people advocating for labor politics or democratic socialist politics in Texas, you’ll often be told, that’s good for California or New York, said Griscom. “But the fact of the matter is that Texas has maybe an even stronger socialist and democratic socialist tradition than some of these other places that we see as the hotbeds for these kind of politics.” That history, said Griscom, cuts against the pervasive idea that Texas will only become more progressive as Californians and New Yorkers move in. Some of these same narratives have resurfaced during this year’s midterm election season. “But most of the data that we have right now actually shows those people are more Republican than the average Texan,” he said. “Just think about some of the famous examples, Joe Rogan and Elon Musk.” As the book notes, polls show that in the 2018 Senate race, more native born Texans voted for Democratic candidate Beto O’Rourke than incumbent Senator Ted Cruz, who won the election. Amid the midterms, there have been some efforts to reclaim the state’s left-populist history, Griscom said. James Talarico, the Democratic Texas state representative and former public school teacher who is now also the Democratic nominee for US Senate, has been telling voters that billionaires are waging “class warfare” against ordinary people – something Griscom has praised. Griscom has, however criticized some of Talarico’s recent moves to cozy up to billionaires like business magnate Mark Cuban, with whom he teamed up on recent policy proposals. “He needs to avoid the siren song of moving to the right economically,” Griscom said. “The way to build that mass appeal, and win a populist coalition, is not by tacking right or pushing technocratic policies no matter what the consultants tell you. Nor is sorting billionaires into good or bad billionaires. The history of populism, and the success of Talarico in the primary is clear, if you want to win Texas you need to mobilize working people with a clear vision of the way politics can improve their life.” The author believes a true return to left populism in Texas will require the buildout of organizations like the Democratic Socialists of America. Though they’ll never have the capital of wealthy far-right political financiers in the state like oilman Tim Dunn, he hopes these organizations can make up for their lack of money with “people power”. “If you look at the history of the Texas populous movement, that was their great advantage,” said Griscom. “They had a rootedness in working-class communities in the state of Texas. That’s what it takes.” In February, he noted, union leader and Democrat Taylor Rehmet won a special election for state senate, flipping a reliably Republican district which Donald Trump won by 17 points in 2024. “It was a real moment of reckoning for the Republican party which got them running scared,” he said.

webTitle: ‘They’re ready to come home’: the movement to bring young voters back to Democrats

fields.headline: ‘They’re ready to come home’: the movement to bring young voters back to Democrats
fields.trailText: After young people shifted right for Trump, Democratic-aligned groups across the US are eager to capture gen Z voters before November’s midterm elections
fields.bodyText: On the first day of the fall semester at California State University, Northridge, student organizers holding “Hot People Vote” signs wheeled a bright pink wagon outside the student union. They offered “no strings attached” donuts, heart-shaped sunglasses and voting information for the November general election. Even though it was 105F outside, dozens of people stopped by to chat with the Donuts + Democracy volunteers and register to vote. One student told organizer Dzian Tran that she didn’t plan to vote because she was disillusioned with politics. Tran chatted with her about how civic engagement is important to democracy and how some elections are won by a margin of only 400 votes. As she thanked Tran, the student held her phone up to a QR code to get more information about voting. About 50 million young people are eligible to vote in 2026, but nearly half are either not registered or civically engaged, according to US Census Bureau data. After Donald Trump made significant gains among young men in the 2024 election, Democratic-aligned groups have been eager to capture gen Z voters who may be disaffected by politics. From bringing politicians, celebrities and donuts to campuses to hosting tailgating events, happy hours and street parties, a crop of youth-led and youth-focused organizations are employing fresh tactics to meet gen Z where they are – and luring them in with fun. Heather Haggarty, who runs Donuts + Democracy with her daughter, said traditional voter engagement strategies such as postcards, clipboards and phone-banking fail with young voters. When her two gen Z children suggested taking donuts to a university voter registration event a few years ago, she ended up speaking to more than 100 kids in 90 minutes. Haggarty said the deep-fried snack is akin to “breaking bread”, making zoomers more willing to talk and connect. “Young kids aren’t apathetic,” she said. “They care. But voting isn’t easy and traditional voter engagement can feel transactional and alienating.” ‘From a quinceañera in Texas to a block party in Philly’ While Republicans invested more than $1bn to target young voters from 2020 to 2025, Democrats haven’t historically backed campus organizing and young organizers, said Haggarty. It’s often left up to young people to inspire and educate their peers. Since 2021, the Keep Arizona Blue Student Coalition, or Keep AZ Blue, has registered about 15,000 students at high schools and colleges. “We engage people online where young people are most, on campus and at community events and coffee shops and other hangout spots,” said Jacob Marson, the group’s 22-year-old executive director. “As football starts up, we’re going to bring elected officials to tailgates along with energy drinks and donuts – these are conversation starters.” Marson’s team has found that community colleges have been largely ignored by organizers in the past. When they show up on those campuses, whether in rural areas or Maricopa county (the fourth-most populous US county), they have “amazing conversations”, Marson said. Last year, Keep AZ Blue brought the Arizona representative Lorena Austin to Mesa Community College, and earlier this year they introduced Arizona’s attorney general, Kris Mayes, to students at Arizona State University. “I think some young voters took a chance on Trump, but it’s clear they’re ready to come home and support our Democratic candidates,” Marson said. “They’ve seen the policies of a Republican-controlled House, Senate and presidency. I am fully confident that young voters are ready to elect Democrats across the state.” Although research has shown that 43% of zoomers do not identify with a political party, they are twice as likely to move left in recent years. And while young people face the most obstacles to voting of any age group, once gen Z is registered to vote, they vote at close to the turnout rates of those over age 30. Youth-focused organizations understand that gen Z voters swing elections. The non-partisan voter organization When We All Vote, founded by Michelle Obama, hosted more than 500 Party at the Polls events throughout the US in 2024. This year, they are scaling up to 5,000 events with a goal of reaching an estimated 20 million gen Z voters. They are particularly focusing on Black and brown communities in the aftermath of the gutting of the Voting Rights Act and other suppression efforts. “It could be anything from a quinceañera in Texas to a block party in Philly to smaller cookouts and barbecues,” said senior adviser Kalisha Dessources Figures. “We’re meeting communities where they are with what looks like joy and celebration to them.” The organization recently brought Love Island USA winner Serena Page to the University of Houston for a conversation on college, dating and civic engagement that was attended by hundreds of students who received free giveaways such as tooth gems and custom merch. HeadCount is another organization mixing voter registration efforts with joy. This year, they have teamed up with celebrities such as Ilana Glazer, Harry Styles and Bob the Drag Queen to encourage gen Z to take action for chances to win tickets and VIP experiences at concerts, sporting events and music festivals. All of this outreach might be helping: some primaries this year have already seen increased turnout among zoomers. In El Paso’s primary, the youth turnout nearly tripled compared to 2022. In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed received almost 60% of the vote in key counties where college-aged voters live, and some experts believe the youth vote was likely responsible for his close primary win. California, meanwhile, has added nearly 2 million more gen Z-aged registered voters since 2022, and more than two-thirds of 18- to 29-year-olds say they are inclined to support progressive candidates in the state. Harnessing anger and frustration Some youth-led organizations are also rallying young people to get more involved in activism, organizing their peers and building political power for their generation. At the recent Voters of Tomorrow summit in Raleigh, North Carolina, hundreds of young people turned out to hear from progressive politicians such as the Tennessee representative Justin Pearson and North Carolina representative Jordan Lopez. Attenders also participated in trainings and workshops on peer-to-peer organizing and building political power online. “We’re working to make sure young people know what’s at stake, but we’re also working with candidates to make sure they are making promises that they can actually deliver on,” said Santiago Mayer, the founder and executive director of Voters of Tomorrow (VOT). “We’ve seen in New York and New Jersey and Virginia and Michigan – young people are looking for candidates who are talking about the issues they need addressed.” The gen Z-led organization has more than 11,000 members and chapters in more than 25 states. In addition to campus events, they have hosted happy hours in Iowa and a film festival in North Carolina to engage new voters. “We’re trying to host events where young people can make new friends and come back not just because they agree with the politics, but because they feel it’s a third space where people can find community and have fun,” said Mayer, who founded VOT in 2019 at age 17. While he said the left was outspent when it came to targeting young voters in 2024, he believes Democrats can win gen Z in the midterms. “Trump lied to them when he said no new wars and that prices would come down,” he said. “Young people do not like being lied to or used, and that’s what Republicans did. They immediately threw us under the bus.”

webTitle: Conflicting court rulings on Missouri map threaten November’s election | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: Conflicting court rulings on Missouri map threaten November’s midterm election
fields.trailText: The state can’t use new congressional districts under one court order – or its old ones under another. Plus, the architects in Europe turning urban spaces into areas of climate respite
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Clashing court rulings plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty less than two months before the November midterms that will decide which party controls a closely divided Congress. Conservative justice Brett Kavanaugh denied the emergency request from Missouri officials to use a congressional map in November that was redrawn with Donald Trump’s support to give Republicans an edge in the midterms, but a ruling by a federal judge in Missouri temporarily prevented the state from using its old congressional maps. Why is there legal action over the maps? The Missouri supreme court has previously ruled that the new map must go before voters to approve or reject the new districts, meaning it cannot be used in time for the November election. The president and Republicans had fumed over the decision, with Trump calling it “horrible, ridiculous, and unconstitutional”. What are the significant changes to the map intended to favor Republicans? The revised map targeted the fifth congressional district, held by longtime Democratic representative Emanuel Cleaver of Kansas City. It reassigned portions of Kansas City to two neighboring districts represented by Republicans and stretched the remainder of Cleaver’s district far eastward into rural Republican areas. Israel to close British consulate in Jerusalem after UK imposes sanctions on West Bank settlements The UK government has entered a diplomatic row with Israel after it announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements. In the country’s starkest condemnation since the founding of the Israeli state, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband – whose mother, Marion Kozak, was a Holocaust survivor who fled to Israel – said settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, claimed the ruling UK Labour party Miliband belongs to was gripped by “Jew hatred”. What has the British prime minister said? Writing in the Guardian, Andy Burnham said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, and that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”. “The measures we are taking,” he said, “are about targeting illegal settlements and increasing the pressure on the Israeli government to change course. We are not imposing sanctions on Israel as a whole.” How has Israel reacted? Israel has ordered the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem among retaliatory measures including entry bans on several UK lawmakers. The Israeli government added that longstanding British involvement in the training of Palestinian security forces on the West Bank would be terminated. Britain will also be excluded from the US-led Gaza coordination mission. US says Iranian tankers ‘destroyed’ as Houthis strike Saudi Arabian cities The US military on Tuesday said it had “destroyed” several Iranian tankers after Iran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles, as violence once again surged across the region, pushing the price of oil past $100 a barrel. Centom said the strikes came after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targeted a US navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the past two days. The IRGC said it had struck a US military base in Jordan in retaliation. What have been the other developments in the region? Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze in what appeared to be a significant expansion of the Middle East war. Saudi Arabia said it would retaliate after the overnight strikes – reportedly involving dozens of drones and missiles – that targeted several oil facilities in the country’s south. US bans Canadian dairy, alcohol and motorcycles as trade war escalates The US is banning dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles from Canada, the White House said on Tuesday, as the trade war between the two neighbors and longtime allies escalates. The ban will take effect in three weeks and comes after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on $20bn in US imports earlier on Tuesday. Donald Trump also moved Tuesday to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term US government contracts. Some Canadian provinces have banned the sale of US alcoholic products – a move that prompted the retaliatory US ban on Tuesday. Canadian tariffs hit hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment. In other news … The pilots of an Amazon cargo plane tried to abort landing in Miami seconds before the crash that killed five employees of an aircraft cleaning company who were in a van it struck. Ex-60 Minutes managing editor Guy Campanile says fired staffers “refused to be accomplices” in the show’s “destruction” under new editorial leadership. The Trump administration plans to confront Australia’s government over its decision that US tech companies must allow users to opt out of social media algorithms. Television programme South Park is to change its name to South America “inspired by bravery and patriotism” of Apple and Google, who capitulated to Donald Trump’s requests to change Lake Ontario to Lake America. Stat of the day: Ukraine books in 1,000 Patriot missiles as UK and EU open up aid Ukraine is ⁠contracting a supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles over the coming years with the help of allies and ⁠through an E⁠U loan, the country’s defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, has said. The development comes as Kyiv faces food shortages after Moscow’s forces continually bomb warehouses supporting civilian life. Well actually: the truth behind ‘old person smell’ No you aren’t imagining it, people do smell different as they get old. Jillian Pretzel gets into the science of why, and whether you can do anything about it. Don’t miss this: Grief, fury, conspiracy – inside Turning Point USA after Charlie Kirk’s killing A year since his assassination, the movement Kirk started is reckoning with the void he left behind - and a revolution that eats its own. … or this: European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss Rafael Behr has a warning that far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism on the continent for another generation. Climate check:the architects clawing back Europe’s car-centric spaces The European Prize for Urban Public Space’s shortlist highlights architectural projects that convert infrastructure for cars into spaces that help urban dwellers cope with the soaring temperatures of the climate crisis: roundabouts that have become splash pools, thoroughfares turned into green havens, and car parks into gardens. Last Thing: Tame Impala frontman announces he will no longer sign autographs due to ‘aggressive’ collectors The Australian musician Kevin Parker has announced he will no longer sign autographs, citing “aggressive” professional collectors who he claimed had used children in order to get his signature. The Tame Impala singer also said he would no longer meet with fans in the parking lot after shows “for the time being” after being warned of “the obvious security risk”. webTitle: US supreme court rejects Missouri Republicans’ appeal to use Trump-backed congressional map in midterms – as it happened

fields.headline: US supreme court rejects Missouri Republicans’ appeal to use Trump-backed congressional map in midterms – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: We’re wrapping up our live coverage for the day. Here are today’s key developments in US politics: Clashing court rulings plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty. The US Supreme Court decided not to intervene to reinstate a Donald Trump-backed US House map, upholding a a ruling from the state’s highest state court that prevented the use of the map in the November elections. But shortly after a federal judge temporarily barred the state from using its old congressional maps in November. The US military destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers after a US navy warship was targeted with ballistic missiles. Iran had targeted the warship twice over two days, the US Central Command said. The US will ban Canadian dairy products, motorcycles and most alcoholic beverages. The move marked an escalation in the ongoing trade war between the North American countries, and comes just after Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on $20bn in US goods. Congressman Chris Pappas beat back progressive challenger Karishma Manzur in the New Hampshire Democratic primary for US Senate. Former senator John E Sununu, who is backed by Trump, won the state’s Republican Senate primary. Lonnie G Bunch III announced he is stepping down as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution after seven years in the role amid Donald Trump’s unprecedented crackdown on the world’s largest museum’s autonomy. Karen Bass plans to step down from the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority Commission. The mayor told the local radio station KFI she would no longer serve on the board because she did not have the time. LAist recently reported that since Bass appointed herself to the governing body in 2023, she had missed more than half of the meetings. The agency has been under scrutiny by the Trump administration. Last week Bass was asked been asked to testify before a congressional committee as part of an investigation into the “potential misallocation” of federal funds by the agency. Congressman Robert Garcia described the move as “another attempt by Donald Trump and House Republicans to launch a witch hunt against Mayor Karen Bass and Los Angeles.” Global oil prices surged to levels last seen in July as the conflict between the US and Iran intensified this week. Oil prices rose to almost $100 a barrel in early Asia trading, shortly after it emerged that the US military “destroyed” multiple Iranian tankers in response to Iran attempting to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles. Read more on today’s developments from the Guardian’s Shrai Popat: Former senator John E Sununu triumphed on Tuesday in the New Hampshire Republican Senate primary Scott Brown, earning the GOP nod in what will likely be a must-win race if Democrats hope to seize the upper chamber. Sununu, 61, was the clear frontrunner in the GOP primary. He served one term in the Senate from 2003 to 2009. Brown represented Massachusetts, later moved to New Hampshire, and served as US ambassador to New Zealand and Samoa during Donald Trump’s first term. The US president threw his support behind Sununu earlier this year, despite the former lawmaker’s past criticism of Trump, including a 2024 op‑ed in which Sununu called Trump a “loser” and backed Nikki Haley in the Republican presidential primary. On the trail, Sununu has tried to show daylight between himself and the administration, criticizing Trump’s tariff policy, urging Congress to rein in executive power, and questioning the decision to launch military action in Iran. Congressman Chris Pappas beat back progressive challenger Karishma Manzur in the Democratic primary for US Senate on Tuesday, advancing as most observers expected to what will be a closely watched general election that is critical to Democratic hopes of flipping the upper chamber. The two were competing for the nomination that opened up after Jeanne Shaheen, 79, the state’s three‑term incumbent Democratic senator, announced her retirement. Pappas, a popular centrist, has served in the House since 2019 and has crossed the aisle at various points. He calls himself “battle‑tested” and has consolidated establishment backing, earning endorsements from leading Democratic lawmakers and former vice‑president Kamala Harris. Missouri’s congressional maps have been thrown into more chaos following a federal judge’s decision to bar the state from using its old congressional maps in the November midterm elections. While Republicans in the state are celebrating the decision, it’s unclear exactly what it will mean for Missouri voters. The Associated Press reports that an attorney for People Not Politicians said another order from Missouri’s supreme court against using the new map remains in effect. “An individual federal judge cannot overrule the Missouri Supreme Court,” said Chuck Hatfield. The US will ban Canadian dairy products, motorcycles and most alcoholic beverages, the White House said on Tuesday. The move marks an escalation in the ongoing trade war between the North American countries, and comes just after Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on $20bn in US goods. Earlier in the day following Canada’s announcement, Trump also announced plans to exclude Canadian products from large US government contracts. The ban is set to take effect in three weeks. Shortly after the US Supreme Court decided not to intervene in the battle over Missouri’s new congressional map earlier today, a federal judge temporarily barred the state from using old districts in the November elections. Last week Missouri’s highest state court blocked the use of a newly drawn congressional map backed by Donald Trump, ruling that voters must approve or reject the new districts. The map had already been used in August primary elections. The decision outraged Donald Trump and Catherine Hanaway, the state’s Republican attorney general, who immediately pledged to appeal to the supreme court. The supreme court, however, turned back the emergency appeal on Tuesday, letting the state court’s ruling stand. But almost immediately after, a federal judge in Missouri issued a temporary restraining order that bars Missouri from using anything other than the new Republican backed map. Hanaway said in a statement that Missouri would “follow and comply” with the judge’s order. “We maintain that changing the congressional map in between the primary and general elections is simply not feasible and profoundly unjust to Missouri voters,” she said. The US military destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers after a US navy warship was targeted with ballistic missiles. Iran had targeted the warship twice over two days, the US Central Command said in a statement on Tuesday. The ship evaded the attacks and no personnel were harmed, according to the statement. Speaking from Colombia, secretary of state Marco Rubio said if Iran attacks US warships, the US military will hit Iranian oil tankers. “Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and ‌for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re ⁠going to lose tankers,” Rubio told reporters. The US Supreme Court decision not to reinstate a Donald Trump-backed US House map in Missouri is a blow to Republicans and the president’s mid-decade redistricting effort. Missouri was the second Republican state to act in response the president’s push to redraw congressional maps to favor Republicans. Mike Kehoe, the state’s governor, called the legislature into a special session last year to create new boundaries ahead of the US midterm elections. The state utilized the new map in its primary elections in August. But last week the state’s supreme court, which includes five Republican-appointed judges, ‌unanimously ruled voters must approve the map in November before it can be utilized. The state’s attorney general argued the decision thrust Missouri into a “full‑fledged constitutional crisis”. The US supreme court will not suspend a ruling from Missouri’s highest state court that prevented the use of a Donald Trump-backed US House map in an upcoming election. Last week the state’s supreme court ruled that the map must go before voters to approve or reject the new districts, meaning it cannot be used in the November election. Trump and Republicans fumed over the decision, with the president calling it “horrible, ridiculous, and unConstitutional”. Catherine Hanaway, the state’s Republican attorney general, immediately pledged to appeal to the supreme court. The conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh denied the emergency request. Senator Alex Padilla praised Lonnie Bunch III, the outgoing Smithsonian chief, for his “longstanding service” and “telling the full story of America”. “Secretary Bunch has been instrumental in telling and preserving the story of our nation and our culture, putting truth and accuracy over politics,” the Democratic lawmaker said in a statement. “In the face of Donald Trump’s attacks on the Smithsonian, Secretary Bunch spoke truth to power and reasserted his commitment to defend and uphold American history and values.” Lonnie G Bunch III has announced he is stepping down as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution after seven years in the role amid Donald Trump’s unprecedented crackdown on the world’s largest museum’s autonomy. In an interview with the New York Times (paywall), Bunch, 73, said it was not the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to control how the Smithsonian presents US history and values that had led to his departure. In response to the news that Lonnie Bunch III will step down as chief of the Smithsonian Institution, some Republicans have assailed his tenure leading the storied collection of museums. “Good riddance,” wrote Josh Hawley, a GOP senator from Missouri. The lawmaker and fierce defender of Donald Trump said that Bunch “should return his salary to the American people”. Meanwhile, Democrats have praised Bunch for his seven years leading the organization. “He is a student of history who has devoted his life to telling America’s full history and cultivating our nation’s continued love of learning and exploration,” said Senator Catherine Cortez Masto, a Democrat from Nevada, who serves on the Smithsonian’s 17-member board and will be responsible to selecting his replacement. US Central Command (Centcom) said that a submarine drone, that Iranian forces claimed to have captured, actually “malfunctioned more than a day ago”. In a statement to the Guardian by US Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, a Centcom spokesperson, said that the underwater drone was surveying regional waters in support of the ongoing military operation in the region. Hawkins said the submersible was “defective” and an older model. He also downplayed that it was a sophisticated piece of technology, adding that it “neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”. Marco Rubio said today that US is “not going to do what the UK did” and impose sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements, but stopped shy of commenting on the matter while speaking to reporters today. However, the secretary of state said that the US does not “want to see some uptick in violence or an uptick in conflict or tensions in the West Bank at a very tenuous time in the region”. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that New York City would release 170,000 pages of previously undisclosed documents that show officials at the time knew that the air quality after the 9/11 terror attacks posed health risks, despite assuring the public and first responders that the air quality was safe. Ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks, the city has published the documents to a publicly accessible portal, which includes air quality reports and correspondence between New York officials. Mamdani directed $34m of the city’s budget to create the portal for the records. Democrats have hit back against Donald Trump’s suggestion that the state of New Mexico should be renamed “New America”, accusing the US president of trying to distract from his war on Iran and rising prices. Michelle Lujan Grisham, the state’s Democratic governor said in a post on X that New Mexico’s name “isn’t up for debate – it’s been ours since before the United States existed.” She added: “While the President tries to distract Americans from his disastrous war in Iran, gas prices keep soaring.” More here The court of appeals for the District of Columbia upheld a block by a lower court judge that prevents the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) from sharing tax return information with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The court also noted that IRS’ argument against the preliminary injunction – namely that it “impedes and delays federal law enforcement by improperly restricting the information that ICE is entitled to receive” – is actually a problem that needs to be addressed through legislation in Congress, not the court. The judges added that the administration’s claim is “weak sauce”. The court of appeals for the District of Columbia upheld a block by a lower court judge that prevents the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) from sharing tax return information with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). “No statute authorizes the IRS to disclose ‘return information’ for non-tax civil investigations without the taxpayer’s consent, or to disclose ‘taxpayer return information’ for any purpose,” the court writes in its ruling. The court also noted that IRS’ argument against the preliminary injunction – namely that it “impedes and delays federal law enforcement by improperly restricting the information that ICE is entitled to receive” – is actually a problem that needs to be addressed through legislation in Congress, not the court. The judges added that the administration’s claim is “weak sauce”. Last year, the IRS established the “Data-Exchange Procedure” with ICE, which provides the agency with the last-known addresses of 1.2 million taxpayers who may be undocumented. Soon after the plaintiffs challenged the new policy, blocked the data sharing, which the government appealed. US Central Command (Centcom) said that a submarine drone, that Iranian forces claimed to have captured, actually “malfunctioned more than a day ago”. In a statement to the Guardian, US Navy Capt Tim Hawkins, a Centcom spokesperson, said that the underwater drone was surveying regional waters in support of the ongoing military operation in the region. Hawkins said the submersible was “defective” and an older model. He also downplayed that it was a sophisticated piece of technology, adding that it “neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment”. Hawkins added that operations in area waters continue. Earlier today, Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to Iranian state TV that its naval forces “captured one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines of the US terrorist army at the entrance to the strait of Hormuz”. They added that the drone was “equipped with the latest technology”. In response to the news that Lonnie Bunch III will step down as chief of the Smithsonian Institution, several Republicans have assailed his tenure leading the storied collection of museums. “Good riddance,” wrote Josh Hawley, a GOP senator from Missouri. The lawmaker and fierce defender of Donald Trump said that Bunch “should return his salary to the American people”. Similarly, Congressman Brandon Gill – a hardline conservative from Texas – said that he was “glad to see” Bunch retire. “The days of using America’s museums to teach Americans to hate their own country are coming to an end,” Gill said on X. “New leadership must tell America’s story accurately.” As we reported earlier, Trump has spent much of his second term in office undermining the content, programming and leadership of Smithsonian, including signing an executive order to “restore” the institution to “its rightful place as a symbol of inspiration and American greatness”. Democrats, however, have praised Bunch for his seven years leading the organization. “He is a student of history who has devoted his life to telling America’s full history and cultivating our nation’s continued love of learning and exploration,” said Senator Catherine Cortez Masto, a Democrat from Nevada, who serves on the Smithsonian’s 17-member board and will be responsible to selecting his replacement. Meanwhile, Representative Terri Sewell, a Democrat from Alabama, thanked Bunch for his “trailblazing leadership” and appeared to push back on the criticism from Republicans that Bunch had attempted to rewrite American history. Sewell said that the outgoing chief “helped ensure that all Americans can see themselves – and their history – reflected in the Smithsonian”. A US appellate court has decided that the federal constitution does not guarantee a right to clean water. That legal opinion came in the form of a decision on Friday from the fifth circuit court of appeals to uphold a lower court’s dismissal of a 2022 lawsuit from several Jackson, Mississippi, residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their constitutional rights. Those residents of Mississippi’s capital city contended that their local drinking water was unsafe to drink because of high lead levels and other contaminants. The New Orleans-based fifth circuit’s majority opinion held that the residents wanted “recognition of two new constitutional rights lacking any foundation in the history and tradition of our nation” – those being “the right to be free from exposure to contaminated water and the right to accurate information from public officials”. In the majority’s view, residents should have gone about their legal fight for clean water another way, such as pursuing “tort claims” or by “electing representatives who will better manage the public-water system, and petitioning their representatives for other remedies”. Tort claims allege “harms caused by others” while seeking “to impose liability on parties responsible for the harm, and to deter others from committing harmful acts”, according to Cornell University’s law school. Friday’s decision also said that state and federal officials were working hard to improve the majority-Black city’s drinking water. The residents who filed suit alleged that public authorities had for years failed to mitigate lead levels and failed to inform them about an increase. Bunch’s resignation will mark a huge leadership transition at a vulnerable and politically fraught time for the institution. During Trump’s second term in office, the president has repeatedly attacked how the Smithsonian presents US history, starting when he signed an executive order in March last year targeting “divisive narratives” and “improper ideology” at the institution. This progressed into frequent attacks, sweeping exhibition reviews and federal funding threats. Bunch has had to tread a fine line between defending the Smithsonian’s independence and commitment to historical accuracy and complexity, and complying with some of the administration’s demands. Trump has accused the organization of being too “woke” and focusing too much on unsavoury aspects of US history. A recent report prepared by the White House’s domestic policy council called “Saving America’s Story” accused the museum’s leadership of “ideological capture”. The Smithsonian “explicitly adopted an ideological framework that no longer treats the American story as a shared national inheritance to be taught or celebrated, but as a political instrument to divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens”, the report said. In July, Trump then ordered the interior department to display signs in front of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History accusing the institution of “inaccurate information”. Interior secretary Doug Burgum then sent a letter to the Smithsonian last week accusing its leadership of having “sanctioned a radical institutional ideology to permeate” the museum and threatening to cut off executive agencies’ cooperation with the institution if it failed to abandon that agenda. Bunch pushed back against many of the administration’s efforts, reiterating the Smithsonian’s commitment to “scholarship, nonpartisanship, independence, accuracy, and integrity.” But he has also complied with some of the White House’s requests, including handing over extensive documents about museum exhibitions and programming details for review. Lonnie G Bunch III has announced he is stepping down as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution after seven years in the role amid Donald Trump’s unprecedented crackdown on the world’s largest museum’s autonomy. In an interview with the New York Times (paywall), Bunch, 73, said it was not the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to control how the Smithsonian presents US history and values that had led to his departure. It was really just saying, now’s the time. I’m a fighter. But, acknowledging the strain of the role, he added: I have to be honest, it has been stressful. And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone. Bunch, the institution’s first black secretary, is expected to leave the role at the end of the year. The Trump administration has asked the supreme court to allow it to ‌use a revamped immigration database for checking the accuracy of state voter rolls, one of a series of actions that boosts federal involvement in ⁠voting ahead of November’s midterm elections, Reuters reports. Justice department lawyers asked the court to halt a Washington DC-based federal judge’s June ruling that blocked the mass voter verification system, which the judge said was haphazardly assembled and contained unreliable citizenship data. “The district ‌court ⁠has issued an indefensible order that threatens the integrity of upcoming elections by vacating the federal government’s authority to internally use ⁠Social Security data when fulfilling its duty to respond to requests by states to verify ⁠the citizenship of individuals for voting and other purposes,” DOJ lawyers ⁠wrote in a filing. The lawyer of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts woman accused of killing her three young children, has said he hopes Donald Trump will pardon his client after her trial recently ended with a deadlocked jury. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, made the appeal on a televised interview on the ABC show Good Morning America today. The plea comes to Trump after a judge on Friday declared a mistrial after the jury in the Clancy case could not reach a unanimous verdict on whether she was guilty or not guilty, opening the way for another trial. Reddington said he hoped that the president would “consider a pardon” for Clancy given “the type of person she is” and “what she has been through”. “Mr President, I would hope that you would consider this young lady,” said Reddington, who also alluded to how Trump on Friday called the case a “tragedy”. Trump’s pardon powers are applicable in the federal justice system in the US, and Clancy was tried in Massachusetts’ state criminal justice system. The president was asked about the trial by reporters on Friday, with Trump calling the case “a shame” and a “horrible tragedy”. “I think the judge has said it’s going to be a mistrial, so there’s going to be another trial,” he said. “It’s a terrible situation. Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. “Can’t be worse. But you’ll find out what the price to pay is. There’ll be a price. It’s going to be mental institution or jail or something, but I guess they’re going to go through another trial.” Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed said they seized an American submarine drone “equipped with the latest technology” in the strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. “The IRGC naval forces captured one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines of the US terrorist army at the entrance to the strait of Hormuz in a complex intelligence and operational action at dawn today,” the Guards said in a statement carried by Iranian state TV. “This submarine has now been captured and images of it will be released in the coming hours.” The White House did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. In January, the New York police department’s counter-terrorism unit sent out a memo warning police officers about a new potential “security and counterintelligence” threat: Ray-Ban Meta glasses. The memo directed officers to “conduct thorough inspections of all eyewear permitted within inmate cells” and cautioned that people who have been arrested could use these glasses, equipped with small cameras and microphones, to record inside police facilities. The memo cited two examples of such videos posted on social media. “The ability to covertly record inside a law enforcement or detention facility, could result in a security risk if proprietary information about cell layouts, camera placements, or officer patrol/site protection routines are released,” the memo read. The NYPD memo is one of a dozen, previously unreported and reviewed by the Guardian, that showed law enforcement agencies across the US are increasingly concerned about the potential for smart glasses to be used against them. Officers from Maine to California worry the technology will be used either to secretly record officers and facilities or to aid in the execution of crimes and acts of terrorism. One of the videos, taken with smart glasses and posted to TikTok in July 2025, offered a rare peek into a South Carolina detention center that had been the subject of a federal investigation over unsafe conditions. “Everyone here is trying to figure out what’s going on with my glasses, why my light is blinking,” the user said about other detainees in the video. “People don’t know about Meta glasses.” He filmed a dingy shower, the inside of holding cells, an overcrowded cafeteria, and several other detainees as they slept, ate or walked, all seemingly unaware of being recorded. US police and federal agents are not alone in their fear. Concern among the public and privacy experts over Meta’s smart glasses, widely dubbed “pervert glasses”, is growing. The technology enables its wearers to record people without their consent and has already been used to harass people.
